title: The August Stock Order That Locks In an Importer's Christmas Margin
linkedin:
Most Australian importers know their Christmas margin depends on the exchange rate. Fewer treat that as something decided in August, not December.

By the time Christmas stock is trading in November, the landed cost is already locked. Production time, sea freight and customs clearance typically add eight to twelve weeks, so the purchase order going out this winter fixes the foreign currency cost of the goods months before a single unit sells.

Here's the part that catches most owners out. Retail and wholesale pricing is usually set well before the true landed cost is known. If the Australian dollar moves, freight capacity tightens into peak season, or a supplier's FOB price shifts between deposit and balance payment, that change lands on the margin quietly. It rarely gets noticed until the January reconciliation, long after the trading period that mattered most has closed.

The businesses that come out of Christmas with the margin they modelled are not the ones who got lucky on the exchange rate. They are the ones who treated the currency exposure as a decision to make at the point of ordering, not a number to discover at the point of reconciling.

If your business places a bulk Christmas order overseas, this is worth thirty minutes with your numbers before the next purchase order goes out.

For Brisbane and east coast businesses that import stock for Christmas trading, August is when this year's Christmas margin actually gets decided, not December.

Most Christmas orders placed with overseas suppliers this month will not land until October or November, once production time, sea freight and customs clearance are accounted for. That means the exchange rate used today, along with freight costs and customs duty, becomes the landed cost the business is stuck with once the stock arrives, regardless of what happens to the Australian dollar between now and then.

The businesses that protect their margin through this period tend to treat currency risk as something to manage at the time the order goes out, rather than something to discover once the invoices are reconciled after Christmas trading finishes.

If you are an import-reliant retailer, wholesaler or online seller on the east coast placing bulk stock orders this month, it is worth taking a proper look at how your landed cost is calculated before the next purchase order is sent.
